Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

Negative Appraisals.value: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
Adwoa is a 74-year-old agricultural worker who lives with her partner on a small farm in the rural South. She is from Ghana originally, and the soil and open fields that once felt like home have become a landscape of dread. The rape happened three years ago, just after dusk, when a man she knew caught her alone in the storage shed behind the main house. She remembers the smell of damp earth and turned hay, the sudden stillness when he blocked the door, and the weight of his hands on her body. In the weeks that followed, she stopped going near the shed after sunset. She began to avoid the dark altogether, staying inside well before nightfall, and she flinched at any unexpected touch from her partner-a hand on her shoulder, a gentle pat on the back. The anniversary of that evening sends her into a spiral, but it is the everyday triggers that keep the wound open. But her own avoidance had begun to multiply the triggers: every path she rerouted, every hour spent indoors before dusk, every time she turned away from a friendly touch-each became a fresh reminder of what she was avoiding, etching the event deeper into her daily landscape.

The smell of soil, especially after a rain, or the brief, complete silence that sometimes falls in the middle of a conversation-these moments flood her with a familiar shame. She will then catch herself forcing her mind to shift, telling herself sternly that she must think only of good things, of the harvest, of her partner's kindness. This positive reframing feels like a duty, but it never lasts. Immediately afterward, the shame returns, heavier than before, because she knows she is lying to herself. She feels dirty, as though the contamination is still on her skin, and she becomes acutely aware of her own body as something ruined. She has come to believe that her life is not worth living anymore, a thought that settles quietly in her chest like a stone. Because she now saw her body as fundamentally irredeemable, the smell of damp earth no longer simply recalled the shed - it landed as proof, a signal she could not ignore, and the same was true of any sudden silence: where once it might have passed unnoticed, now it snapped her attention like a warning.

Her avoidance of touch has deepened into a near-constant vigilance. She stands at a distance from her partner, and when he reaches for her hand she pulls away, her face soft with apology. The more she avoids touch, the more she feels isolated and contaminated, and the more she craves the very contact she fears. This cycle tightens around the anniversary: as the date approaches, she notices the silence more sharply-the way the house goes quiet at midday, the pause between bird calls-and her shame intensifies. She tells herself she should be grateful she survived, that she should be thankful for her partner, but the forced positivity only amplifies her sense of fraudulence and the conviction that her body is beyond redemption.

At work, she now only tends crops in full daylight and always with someone nearby. The smell of turned soil, once the smell of morning, now smells of that shed. She endures it by mentally reciting prayers, but the effort exhausts her. She has stopped volunteering for early shifts, and her supervisor has noticed her reluctance. Her partner, patient at first, has grown confused by her constant refusal of affection. She cannot explain it. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last month, standing alone in the field at noon, when a sudden silence fell-no wind, no machines, no birds-and she felt the same helpless terror as that evening. She realized then that the life she had been forcing herself to believe in was not returning. She is afraid that if she lets go of the positive thoughts, the shame will swallow her entirely. But she is also afraid of staying as she is.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals influence or lead to triggers; triggers are described as external cues that cause negative appraisals rather than the reverse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals influence or lead to triggers; triggers are described as external cues that cause negative appraisals rather than the reverse.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
